newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: First casualties feared from Montserrat volcano.
newsitem.headline: First casualties feared from Montserrat volcano.

text.p: An active volcano in Montserrat spewed ash and rock over much of the island on Wednesday, leaving 17 people unaccounted for and six suffering from burns, officials in the British territory said.

"We're keeping our fingers crossed, but for the first time we fear we may have casualties," Franklin Michael, permanent secretary of the island's Emergency Operations Center, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
He said about a half dozen people had been treated at the island's hospital for minor burns. Monsterrat is a British colony in the eastern Caribbean, about 25 miles (40 km) southwest of Antigua.

Michael said the 17 people considered unaccounted for had been reported missing by relatives or friends, adding that the government had compiled no official data and hoped to be able to report more after another search at first light on Thursday.

Between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. EDT (1700 and 1800 GMT) on Wednesday, part of the giant dome of volcanic material that has been growing inside Montserrat's Soufriere Hills volcano collapsed. This doused much of the island with ash and sent toward eastern Montserrat a pyroclastic flow -- a fast-moving rain of superheated gases, ash and rock that can burn everything in its path.
"There is apparently extensive property damage," Michael said.

Scientists monitoring the volcano said they did not consider the activity to be an explosive event, such as an eruption. However, they ordered an evacuation of the island's airport and sent out helicopters to survey the area and look for anyone who might have been caught.
They said the volcano seemed to have settled down, reporting no comparable activity since the afternoon's event.

The areas believed to have been hit hardest on Wednesday were the villages of Harris, Dyers, Bethel, Farms and Trants, all in the so-called "danger zone", which has been evacuated since April 1996, Michael said.
Southern and eastern Montserrat, including its capital, Plymouth, have been evacuated repeatedly since its volcano roared to life in July 1995 after centuries of virtual dormancy.
The island has seen its population drop to about 6,800 from 11,000 since the volcano began to rumble. Its economy and tourism business also have been hit hard by the disaster.

Some residents of the evacuated areas have refused to leave their homes and others had made periodic visits back to the evacuated area to check on their property and feed animals who could not be evacuated. "A few people could have been caught just when going back to check on property," Michael said.
